title: Best CCPA & California Privacy Tools Compared
metaDescription: Compare CCPA compliance platforms for California privacy law: consumer requests, data mapping, cookie consent, reporting and integrations.
intro: California's privacy law (the CCPA, as amended by the CPRA) gives consumers rights to know, delete, correct and opt out, and requires covered businesses to honor them. This page compares three business platforms for handling those requests, consent and data mapping.

verdict.summary: OneTrust scores highest on this page's six criteria: it covers consumer requests, data mapping, cookie consent, reporting and integrations, though, like the other two, it takes work to set up. TrustArc is second: it matches OneTrust on consumer requests and integrations, with 300+ no-code connectors for fulfilling requests, but scores lower on data mapping, cookie consent and reporting. Privacera ranks third because it is a data-governance tool rather than a full CCPA suite: it is strong at finding, classifying and masking personal data, but it has no cookie consent or consumer request portal.

pro_tips: Start with a data audit before choosing a compliance tool - understanding what personal data you collect helps determine which features you actually need.
Look for platforms that offer both automated and manual request processing, as some consumer requests may require human review for accuracy.
Consider tools that provide consumer-facing portals, making it easier for California residents to exercise their privacy rights without contacting your support team.
Ensure your chosen platform handles the CPRA amendments in force since 2023, including sensitive personal information protections, not just the original CCPA rules.

For consumers: turn on Global Privacy Control in a browser that supports it (covered businesses must treat it as an opt-out of sale and sharing), and use the state's DROP platform to send one deletion request to every registered data broker.

faqs.question: What's the difference between CCPA and CPRA compliance tools?
faqs.answer: CPRA (California Privacy Rights Act) expands on CCPA with additional requirements like sensitive personal information protections and stricter consent requirements. Modern compliance tools should support both, but verify that your chosen platform includes CPRA-specific features like sensitive data handling and enhanced consumer rights management.

faqs.question: Do small businesses need expensive enterprise privacy platforms?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily, and many small businesses aren't covered at all. The CCPA applies to for-profit businesses that meet at least one threshold: annual revenue above $26,625,000 (the 2025 inflation-adjusted figure), buying, selling or sharing the personal information of 100,000 or more California consumers or households, or earning half their revenue from selling or sharing it. A covered smaller business can often start with documented manual processes and lighter tools, then move to an automated platform as request volume grows.

faqs.question: How long do I have to respond to CCPA consumer requests?
faqs.answer: Businesses must respond to CCPA requests within 45 days, with a possible 45-day extension if needed. Most compliance platforms include automated workflows and reminders to help meet these deadlines, which is why automated tools are valuable for businesses regularly receiving requests.

faqs.question: Can I use multiple privacy tools together?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many businesses combine tools, for example a platform like OneTrust or TrustArc for consent and request management alongside a data-governance tool like Privacera that finds and controls personal data in their data stores. The key is making sure the tools share information so requests don't fall through the gaps.

faqs.question: What happens if I don't comply with CCPA requirements?
faqs.answer: The California Privacy Protection Agency and the Attorney General can seek fines of up to $2,663 per violation, or $7,988 per intentional violation or violation involving minors' data (2025 inflation-adjusted amounts). Consumers can also sue over certain data breaches caused by poor security, for $107 to $799 per consumer per incident or actual damages. That makes proper compliance tools and processes essential for any covered business serving California residents.
